title: Goethe's Divan
hookLine: Goethe fell in love with Hafiz and wrote his own West-Eastern Divan (1819)
tomorrow: that viral 'Hafiz' quote on your feed. did he write it?

cards: Somewhere on your phone there's a compass. Inés wants the long-night evening to open with everyone standing up, facing east, then turning to face west. Theo groans: corny.
Inés says it isn't her idea. It comes from a German poet who called Hafiz his twin: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.

teach.b: Goethe was already well-known when Joseph von Hammer's German translation of Hafiz's Divan reached him, and he was swept away. He didn't imitate Hafiz.
He answered him, with a whole book of his own, the West-Eastern Divan.

In one poem he tells Hafiz: with you, with you alone, I want to compete; let joy and pain be shared by us, the twins. And in a poem called Talismans he writes, in German: Gottes ist der Orient! Gottes ist der Okzident!

teach.h: GOD'S IS THE EAST AND THE WEST.
teach.b: God's is the East, God's is the West. That line isn't Goethe's invention. It's the Quran, carried into German.
In Pickthall's English: "Unto Allah belong the East and the West, and whithersoever ye turn, there is Allah's Countenance." Here's the teaching inside it.

teach.h: THE QIBLA, AND NO DIRECTION WITHOUT GOD.
teach.b: Muslims pray facing the qibla, toward the Kaaba in Mecca; the same surah sets that direction. And the same verse says that wherever you turn, God's Countenance is there.
Both at once: one way to face together, and no direction God is missing from. Goethe heard that and built his bridge on it.
He wasn't a Muslim; he was a German poet borrowing with open admiration, and the verse stays the Quran's.

how: Muslims face the qibla, toward the Kaaba in Mecca, in prayer, and some use a compass or an app to find it when traveling. Quran 2:115 is recited as a reminder that God is not bound to any one direction.

Joseph von Hammer's translation of the Divan reached him, and he answered with his own.

Muslims face the qibla in prayer; classical commentators tie the verse to cases like travel or not knowing the direction, and it says God's Countenance is wherever you turn.

games.q: a friend watches Muslim coworkers check a compass app before praying, then reads Quran 2:115. 'if God is everywhere, why face one way?' what fits?
o: both: one direction to face together, and no direction God is missing from.
the verse cancels the direction, so facing Mecca is optional now.

games.why: the qibla gives prayer a shared direction; 2:115 says God's Countenance is wherever you turn. Goethe built on the second half.

practice: Stand up and face east, as best you can guess it, for a few slow breaths. Then turn slowly, halfway around, to face west. Notice the room change as you turn, and stay facing west for the rest of the quiet.

carryVoice: Here's the line: east and west, both God's, as Goethe learned it from the Quran. Five days into Hafiz.
